e) Offence complained of : 279/338 IPC f) Plea of the accused : Accused pleaded not guilty g) Final order : Accused is acquitted for the  offence u/s 279/338 IPC h) Date of final order : 20.04.2023  BRIEF STATEMENT OF FACTS FOR THE DECISION CASE OF THE PROSECUTION 1.
Concisely stated, the instant case was registered on the complaint/statement of complainant Jeet Panwar, who was residing on rent at H.No. 5, Gali No.2, Neb Sarai, New Delhi.

On 29.02.2019, at about 05:40 AM, injured Jeet Panwar was going to his office i.e. Globalogic situated in Gurugram,
Haryana, in the vehicle (make Swift Car) of the company bearing registration no. DL-1ZC-1273,
which was being driven by accused Rohit Yadav, in very high speed and a rash and negligent manner.

At about 05:50 AM, when their car reached at Saket Metro Station, alleged driver Rohit Yadav by driving the said vehicle negligently hit the same to a car which was standstill beside metro station from behind.
Consequently, injured Jeet Panwar sustained grievous injuries.
Thereafter, the alleged driver admitted the complainant in Max Hospital.

The injured deposed that Rohit was State vs . Rohit Yadav on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20636251/
1 known to him prior to this incident as usually he used to take injured to his office.

sentences.text: EVIDENCE OF THE PROSECUTION 5.
Prosecution has examined four witnesses i.e. PW1 Sh. Om Prakash, PW2 Jeet Panwar (the complainant), PW3 HC Krishan and PW4 SI Rajender [the investigating officer (IO)].
6. PW1 Sh. Om Prakash, deposed that on 19.02.2019, he along with his brother went to Saket Metro Station in their car bearing registration o. DL-4CAA-6264.

They stopped their car on one side of the road as they were waiting for someone, when one car (make Maruti Swift) bearing registration no.
DL-1ZC-1273, hit their car from back side (right rear side) due to the negligent driving of the said car.
PW1 further alleged that accused Rohit was driving the said car at a very high speed due to which the person seated in the same car sustained injuries.
The alleged driver Rohit got the injured admitted to hospital in a TSR.

Police officials recorded his statement, seized his car, Driving License,
documents of the car of PW1 and arrested the accused.
Thereafter, PW1 got his vehicle released on superdari.
He correctly identified the alleged car and the car of PW1 in the photographs shown to him.
He also correctly identified the accused.
The witness was duly cross-
examined.
7. PW2 Jeet Panwar, complainant/injured in present case, at the time of incident, he was residing in Neb Sarai, New Delhi and was working in Globalogic Gurugram.

He deposed that he used to reach his office in the vehicle (make Swift car) provided by company bearing registration no. DL-1ZC-1273 State vs . Rohit Yadav on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20636251/
2 which was being driven by accused Rohit.

He deposed that on 19.02.2019, at about 05:40 AM,
alleged driver Rohit picked him from his house to reach office in the said car.
He alleged that while driving the said car, the accused Rohit was driving the vehicle in a very rash and negligent manner.

At about 05:50 AM, when they reached near Saket Metro Station, alleged driver hit their car in a car which was standing on the road near Metro Station due to which, the complainant sustained grievous injury.
Thereafter, alleged driver took him to Max Hospital Saket and he remained admitted there for about 5-6 months.
In June 2019, police officials inquired him and recorded his statement.
He correctly identified the accused in the court.
He also correctly identified the alleged car bearing no. DL1ZC1273 and the car which was hit by the accused in the photographs shown to him.
The witness was duly cross-examined.

8. PW3 HC Kishan deposed that on 19.02.2019, on receipt of GD No. 10A by the IO, he along with ASI Rajender went to place of incident, near Saket metro station where they saw two cars in accidental condition and found one person namely Om Prakash standing there who disclosed to them that the car bearing registration no. DL1ZC1273 belonged to alleged driver and the said driver had taken the injured to some unknown hospital in a TSR.
Thereafter, on receipt of GD No.20A, IO left PW3 at the place of incident and he himself went to Max Hospital.

After coming back to the spot,
IO prepared rukka on GD No.10A, handed over the same to PW3 for registration of FIR and sent him to PS.
After registering the same, he returned to the spot and handed over original rukka and copy of FIR to IO as further investigation marked to the IO.

Thereafter, IO seized both the cars, DL of Om Prakash, documents of car bearing no. DL4CAA6264,
DL of accused, documents of alleged car, prepared site plan at the instance of Om Prakash,
interrogated the accused, arrested him and conducted his personal search.
Later on, accused was released on bail.
After returning to PS, they deposited the case property in the malkhana and his statement was recorded by the IO.
He correctly identified the accused in the court.
He also correctly identified the alleged car and the car of Om Prakash in the photographs shown to him.
The witness was duly cross-
examined.
9. PW4 SI Rajender, deposed on the same line as of PW3 HC Kishan.
Additionally, he collected MLC of injured Jeet Panwar but he was opined unfit for statement by the doctor.

Further, he got the mechanical inspection of both the vehicles conducted, collected the reports, verified the documents of both the cars, driving license of both the drivers, added section 338 IPC in the chargesheet after getting opinion of doctor, recorded statement of injured Jeet Panwar, released both the vehicles on superdri as per directions and after preparing the charge-sheet, he filed it in the court.
He correctly identified both the cars in the photographs shown to him.
He also correctly identified the accused.
The witness was duly cross- examined.
STATEMENT / DEFENCE OF THE ACCUSED 10.

In his statement recorded under Section 313 of the Code, the accused stated that he was driving the car on the said date with the speed of about 50 kms/hr and injured Jeet Panwar was also seated in the same car.
He stated that as it was foggy, he could not see the car which was hit.
The accidental vehicle was kept stationery in a No Parking zone and the parking lights were also not on.

As the State vs . Rohit Yadav on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20636251/
3 balloon of the car opened, he did not sustain any injury.
He stated that he is innocent and has been falsely implicated in this case.
Accused examined himself in his defence evidence.
EVIDENCE OF THE DEFENCE 11.
Accused Rohit Yadav deposed in his defence evidence that on 19.02.2019, he alongwith the injured Jeet Panwar was going to the office after picking him (the injured) from his house.
When they reached near Saket, their car hit a car which was standing in No Parking area whose parking lights were also off.
He stated that there was fog on that day and the incident happened as there was no visibility and therefore, injured Jeet Panwar sustained injuries.
He then admitted the injured to the hospital.
The witness was duly cross-examined.
ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS 12.
The record has been thoroughly and carefully perused.
The respective submissions of Sh. Rajat Bansal, learned Assistant Public Prosecutor for State and Sh. Markandey Gupta, Ld. Counsel for the accused have been considered.

13. In order to establish an offence punishable under Section 279 of the IPC, it must be shown that the accused was driving the vehicle on a public road in a rash or negligent way, threatening human life or likely to cause harm or injury to another person.
Where an offence under Section 279 is established, the accused is also culpable under Section 338 where his rash or negligent act causes grievous hurt to any person.
It is an admitted position that the accused was driving the car bearing No. DL-1ZC-1273, which caused the incident on the relevant date.
PW2/victim as well as PW1/eye witness have also deposed that the accused was driving the offending vehicle on the day of the incident.
Therefore, it can be said that it has been proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused was driving the offending vehicle at the time of incident.
15. The MLC of victim Sh. Jeet Panwar is Ex A-1 and the genuineness of the said document has been admitted by accused in his statement under Section 294 CrPC.
Therefore, it is not a matter of dispute that the complainant suffered grievous injury on the date of incident i.e. 19.02.2019.

In fact,
even the Ld. Counsel for the accused has not put any questions to the complainant disputing the nature of injury suffered by him on the said date.

State vs . Rohit Yadav on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20636251/
4 16.

The final issue for determination is whether the prosecution has been able to establish beyond reasonable doubt that the injuries sustained by the complainant were due to the rash negligent driving of the offending vehicle by the accused.

With respect to the question whether the accused was driving the offending vehicle in a rash and negligent manner, the factum of rashness and negligence has to be gathered from the surrounding circumstances.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ravi Kapoor vs. State of Rajasthan [Crl. Appeal No. 1838/2009] inter alia held as under:
"10.

entities.text: Ravi Kapoor vs. State of Rajasthan [Crl. Appeal No. 1838/2009]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In order to examine the merit or otherwise of contentions (b) and (c) raised on behalf of the appellant, it is necessary for the Court to first and foremost examine (a)
what is rash and negligent driving; and (b) whether it can be gathered from the attendant circumstances.
Rash and negligent driving has to be examined in light of the facts and circumstances of a given case.
It is a fact incapable of being construed or seen in isolation.
It must be examined in light of the attendant circumstances.
A person who drives a vehicle on the road is liable to be held responsible for the act as well as for the result.
It may not be always possible to determine with reference to the speed of a vehicle whether a person was driving rashly and negligently.
Both these acts presuppose an abnormal conduct.

Even when one is driving a vehicle at a slow speed but recklessly and negligently, it would amount to 'rash and negligent driving'
within the meaning of the language of Section 279 IPC.
That is why the legislature in its wisdom has used the words 'manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life'.

The preliminary conditions, thus, are that (a) it is the manner in which the vehicle is driven; (b) it be driven either rashly or negligently; and (c) such rash or negligent driving should be such as to endanger human life.
Once these ingredients are satisfied, the penalty contemplated under Section 279 IPC is attracted.

11. 'Negligence' means omission to do something which a reasonable and prudent person guided by the considerations which ordinarily regulate human affairs would do or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person guided by similar considerations would not do.
Negligence is not an absolute term but is a relative one; it is rather a comparative term.
It is difficult to state with precision any mathematically exact formula by which negligence or lack of it can be infallibly measured in a given case.

Whether there exists negligence per se or the course of conduct amounts to negligence will normally depend upon the attending and surrounding facts and circumstances which have to be taken into consideration by the Court.
In a given case, even not doing what one was ought to do can constitute negligence.
12. The Court has to adopt another parameter, i.e., 'reasonable care' in determining the question of negligence or contributory negligence.

The doctrine of reasonable care imposes an obligation or a duty upon a person (for example a driver) to care for the pedestrian on the road and this duty attains a higher degree when the pedestrian happen to be children of tender years.

It is axiomatic to say that while driving a vehicle on a public way, there is an implicit duty cast on the drivers to see that their driving does not endanger the life of the right users of the road, may be either vehicular users or pedestrians.
They are expected to take sufficient care to avoid danger to others.

State vs . Rohit Yadav on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20636251/
5 13.
The other principle that is pressed in aid by the courts in such cases is the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur.

This doctrine serves two purposes - one that an accident may by its nature be more consistent with its being caused by negligence for which the opposite party is responsible than by any other causes and that in such a case, the mere fact of the accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.
Secondly, it is to avoid hardship in cases where the claimant is able to prove the accident but cannot prove how the accident occurred.
The courts have also applied the principle of res ipsa loquitur in cases where no direct evidence was brought on record.
The Act itself contains a provision which concerns with the consequences of driving dangerously alike the provision in the IPC that the vehicle is driven in a manner dangerous to public life.
Where a person does such an offence he is punished as per the provisions of Section 184 of the Act.
The courts have also taken the concept of 'culpable rashness' and 'culpable negligence' into consideration in cases of road accidents.

'Culpable rashness' is acting with the consciousness that mischievous and illegal consequences may follow but with the hope that they will not and often with the belief that the actor has taken sufficient precautions to prevent their happening.
The imputability arises from acting despite consciousness (luxuria).

'Culpable negligence' is acting without the consciousness that the illegal and mischievous effect will follow, but in circumstances which show that the actor has not exercised the caution incumbent upon him and that if he had, he would have had the consciousness.
The imputability arises from the neglect of civic duty of circumspection.
In such a case the mere fact of accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.

This maxim suggests that on the circumstances of a given case the res speaks and is eloquent because the facts stand unexplained, with the result that the natural and reasonable inference from the facts, not a conjectural inference, shows that the act is attributable to some person's negligent conduct.
[Ref. Justice Rajesh Tandon's 'An Exhaustive Commentary on Motor Vehicles Act, 1988' (First Edition, 2010]."
17. The case of the prosecution is that the accused was driving the offending vehicle in a rash and negligent manner at a high speed and hit the car of PW1, which was parked on one side of the road.
Due to the impact with the stationery car of PW1, the victim/PW2 incurred injuries.
It is pertinent to note that PW1 in his examination in chief dated 20.10.2022 has deposed that he had stopped his car outside the Saket Metro Station as they were waiting for someone.
PW1 has admitted that the vehicle was not parked in the parking area.

The Ld. Counsel for accused has placed reliance on the decision of the Hon'ble Gauhati High Court in Reliance General Insurance Company Limited vs.
Smiti Paul Hazarika and others (Case No. MACApp. 376/2018)

has observed:
"In the case of Ramanna (supra) cited by the Learned counsel for the appellant, it was held that with regard to contributory negligence is concerned, the driver was not supposed to park the lorry on the National Highway.
In case of exigency, if the driver of the lorry is forced to park the lorry on the National Highway, he has to put the indicators.
No evidence has been placed to show that the driver of the lorry had put on the indicators."

18. The Hon'ble High Court of Gujarat in Premlata Nilamchand Sharma vs. Hirabhai Ranchhodbhai Patel (1983 ACJ 290) and the Hon'ble High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Nirmal Chutani vs.
Haryana (1983 ACJ 640) and Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Pushpa Rani Chopra vs. Anokha Singh (1975 ACJ 396) has held that where the place was dark and where the vehicle was parked without State vs . Rohit Yadav

6 any sign or indication to warn other road users, the negligence is on the driver of the parked vehicle and not the driver of any vehicle which dashes into such parked vehicle.

19. It is pertinent to note that Section 122 of the Motor Vehicles Act casts a duty on the driver of a stationary vehicle on a public place so as not to cause any danger, obstruction or undue inconvenience to the users of public place and also to other passengers.

In Kumari Jyothi and others vs. Mohd. Usman Ali and others (ILR 2002 KAR 393) it has been held that the owner of the vehicle has the right to drive the vehicle on the road and also the right to park the vehicle, but the parking of the vehicle cannot cause any danger or obstruction to other passers-by or passengers.

entities.text: Kumari Jyothi and others vs. Mohd. Usman Ali and others (ILR 2002 KAR 393)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This is a restriction on the road to park the vehicle.
The aforesaid restriction on the road to park a vehicle is a reasonable restriction and emanates from a duty to take care.
20. In this context, it was the duty of the prosecution to prove that PW-1 had exercised due care and had parked his car at the right place.
Admittedly, the car was parked on the road at 6 a.m. in the morning.

Whilst PW1 deposed that the parking lights were on, he has not mentioned this in his statement nor has brother (who was present at Saket Metro station) been examined as a witness to depose w.r.t. to said fact.
21. PW1 has deposed that he does not know anything about the site plan.
PW2 has also deposed that he did not go to the place of incident with the police officials.

In view of this, it is averred by Ld.
Counsel for accused that as there is no clarity as to when PW1 or PW2 accompanied the investigating officials to the place of incident, there is credit to the submission that the site plan has been prepared whimsically by the police officials and is not credible.
Moreover, signatures of the complainant is not present in the site plan nor has PW1 deposed that the complainant accompanied the police officials while site plan was prepared.

With respect to the site plan, the Learned counsel for accused has relied on Vijay Singh vs. State of Madhya Pradesh [2005 CrLJ 299], wherein the Hon'ble High Court held that preparation of site plan is not a mere formality, but, it is an essential feature in order to reach the firm conclusion by the court in order to ascertain whether the offence has been committed by accused or not.

entities.text: Vijay Singh vs. State of Madhya Pradesh [2005 CrLJ 299]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The Ld. Counsel for accused has also relied on State vs. Sunil Kumar @Sagar @ Rahul and others [2015 (2) JCC 802] wherein the importance of site plan was stressed and it was observed that:
"Trial Court has pointed out that the site plan is a vital part of the investigation and that it should give a clear description of the spot to which it belongs but the site plan relied upon by the prosecution nowhere shows existence of adjoining houses or shop where public persons where public persons could have been found.

entities.text: State vs. Sunil Kumar @Sagar @ Rahul and others [2015 (2) JCC 802]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Also no attempt is shown to have made to join any public person during the entire investigation."
22.

This court is not blind to the nature of permanently incapacitating injuries which have been incurred by the victim, however, in this Court's considered opinion the negligence of the accused driver is not criminally culpable in nature.

Whilst it is bereft from reality in the Indian context to expect vehicle owners and drivers to not park on the road, but criminal negligence cannot be pinned universally on persons who collide with such vehicles.
This case also highlights the pivotal importance of the rule making wearing of seat belt in the rear seat of the car mandatory.

The State vs . Rohit Yadav on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20636251/
7 prosecution has not been able to establish that the accused was driving the vehicle in a criminally rash and negligent manner.
The ingredients of Sections 279 and 338 of the IPC are not proved.

Consequently, the accused is acquitted of the offences punishable under Sections 279 and 338 of the IPC.
23.
In compliance to Section 437A of the Code, the accused is directed to furnished bail bond and surety bond.
24. File be consigned to Record Room.
